Saturn has 293 confirmed moons in its orbit as of August 2026, far more than any other planet in our solar system.

Saturn's moons range in size, from one that is larger than the planet Mercury — the giant moon Titan — to others as small as a sports arena. The small moon Enceladus has a global ocean under a thick, icy shell. Scientists have identified both moons as high-priority science destinations for future deep-space missions.

Juno's orbits around Jupiter are counted in “perijoves” — the point in each trip around the planet when the spacecraft is closest to Jupiter. In contrast, an “apojove” is the point in its orbit when Juno is farthest from Jupiter. When the spacecraft arrived on July 4, 2016 (PDT) and entered the grasp of the giant planet, the mission team began marking perijoves with that first close encounter — “Perijove 0.”

After that, the spacecraft reached “Apojove 0” on July 31 – when, for the first time, it crossed that most distant point in its circuit around Jupiter, about 5 million miles away from the planet (8.1 million kilometers). NASA’s planetary science missions near the end of their prime mission (PM) or extended mission (EM) may propose an extension. These extended missions can leverage NASA’s large investment in order to perform continued science operations at a cost far lower than developing a new mission. In some cases, the extensions allow missions to continue to acquire valuable long-duration datasets, while in other cases, EMs allow missions to visit new targets, with entirely new science goals. The ‘Senior Review’ of these proposals typically happens every three years, by a panel made of experts from academia, NASA, and industry.

DOC_011193,nasa_science,Uranus Moons,https://science.nasa.gov/uranus/moons/,2960,0.15,"Uranus has more than two dozen officially recognized moons.
Uranus has 29 officially recognized moons, as of August 2026, including five major moons: Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon.

The moons are sometimes called the ""literary moons"" because they are named for Shakespearean characters, along with a couple of the moons being named for characters from the works of Alexander Pope.
The most recently discovered moon was first spotted in November 2023. It's currently designated at S/2023 U1, and will eventually be named for a literary character like the other moons of Uranus.

## Dr. Sue Smrekar, VERITAS Principal Investigator
Dr. Smrekar is a senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California. She is an internationally recognized expert on the surface and interior of Venus.

Her work focuses on understanding the key factors that cause terrestrial planets, especially Venus and Earth, to evolve along different paths. Dr. Smrekar's research integrates geophysical modeling, data analysis, and geologic constraints.
Dr. Smrekar has assembled a diverse science team of leading experts from around the world for the VERITAS mission.
